sheet.title: Happy Thanksgiving from Brennan’s, 3 Courses $80: choice of appetizer, entrée and dessert
sheet.line: Cane Syrup Glaze, Polenta, Mustard Greens, Roasted Apples
sheet.note: The sheet prints the dish name and its line and nothing else: no allergen marks, no price of its own (the $80 covers three courses), no method, no portion, no wine.

classic.tenderloin: Pork tenderloin is very lean and very tender, with a mild flavor; wrapping it in bacon protects it while it roasts, the bacon fat bastes it and adds smoke and salt (America’s Test Kitchen, Bacon-Wrapped Pork Tenderloin Medallions; Tasting Table, Wrap Your Pork Tenderloin In Bacon).
classic.caneSyrup: Cane syrup is sugar cane juice boiled down with nothing taken out, sweeter and milder than molasses, a Louisiana pantry staple used to glaze meat (the pack’s cane syrup component and its sources).
classic.polenta: Polenta comes from the grain mushes of Roman times (puls, pulmentum); maize reached Italy from the Americas in the sixteenth century, and polenta is now usually yellow cornmeal, ground finer than grits; grits come from the Native peoples of the American Southeast, the Muscogee or Creek among them (Wikipedia, Polenta; MasterClass, Polenta vs. Grits; Food Network, Grits vs Polenta).
classic.mustardGreens: Mustard greens are the leaves of Brassica juncea; the curly Southern type is a staple of Southern and soul food cooking, braised slowly with smoked meat; peppery when raw, mellower and sweeter when cooked; the braising liquid is the potlikker (FoodPrint, Real Food Encyclopedia: Mustard Greens; MasterClass, How to Cook Mustard Greens).

sayIt: Polenta: poh-LEN-tuh, the Italian word, from the Latin puls and pulmentum.
unsourced: The pork’s cooking temperature, how the apples are roasted, how the greens are cooked and whether the polenta is soft or set: asked of the chef.
Where the tenderloin sits in the animal: one search gave no source for it, so the notes do not place it.
